asDecan.p: Your Sun sits between ten and nineteen degrees of Scorpio, the middle of the sign's three ten-degree decans, and the Golden Dawn gives that slice to the Sun. So your Sun is sitting in a patch of sky the Sun itself looks after, which I always like. It has no special dignity in Scorpio, mind you. It's a visitor, neither helped nor held back, and it takes on the colour of Mars, the sign's old ruler, and Pluto, the modern one. Mid-sign is where Scorpio is settled and at full strength, fixed water that keeps a feeling for decades, and the Sun adds warmth and a wish to be seen. The Five of Cups before you is Mars, somebody staring at spilt cups. The Seven after you is Venus, daydreams and too many options. Yours is where old feeling gets kept warm, and the picture shows it, a child in an old courtyard handing another a cup of flowers. Death is still your Sun card, as Scorpio's Major. The Six narrows it to your ten degrees.

You keep things. There's a shoebox, or a folder on your phone, with the birthday card from 2009 and a voicemail from your nan you've never been able to delete. At a family dinner you're the one who brings up the caravan holiday where the tent flooded, and you can still say who was sulking and why. Years into a relationship you'll mention what they ordered on your first date, and it slightly unnerves them. When an old friend takes a week to answer a message you notice, and you don't say anything, but you notice. The Sun likes to be at the centre of things, and in this slice that means being the one everyone checks the story with. A wet Saturday can turn into three hours of old photos, and it ends with you messaging somebody from Year 8 to ask if they remember that music teacher.

Plenty of Scorpios can cut a person off and never look back, and you can do it too. The less expected thing is how good you are at going back. The Sun in this slice gives you a way in that the other two decans don't have, and you can look at an old hurt properly and still find something in it worth keeping. You're the one who messages the friend you fell out with at nineteen, fifteen years on, and somehow it lands, because you remembered the good bits accurately and said so. Families lean on this in you without quite noticing. When two siblings haven't spoken since the funeral, it's usually someone like you who rings them both, and who knows which story about their dad will get them laughing on the phone.

You tend to get attached to the version of people you met first. Your best friend from school moves to Perth, makes new friends, gets into trail running and starts saying things differently, and some part of you takes it personally, as if they've walked out on the old version of themselves and on you along with it. You won't say so. You'll just go a bit cool on the phone. It happens with places too, the pub that got done up, the band that changed its sound. And there's a quiet ledger under the generosity. You give a lot and you give well, but you remember every bit of it, and if it isn't returned in kind it can sit for years before it comes out in one sharp sentence, in an argument about something else entirely.

When something goes badly you go backwards first. Bad news, a loss, a week of being overlooked, and you're on the couch with the film you loved at twelve, eating what your mum made when you were home sick. That's fine for a night or two. By the end of the week it's turned into digging. You're reading old messages at one in the morning for the point it went wrong, or you've texted an ex who has nothing to do with it, because they knew you when things were simpler. The Sun here wants warmth, and when it can't find any this week it goes looking in old places. The people who are around you start to feel like they're standing outside a closed door. What helps is someone who's known you for years, sitting with you in daylight, and one small job you can finish with your hands.

You love through shared history, and a relationship gets better for you the longer it runs. The inside jokes, the ticket stubs, the fact that they know which aunt not to bring up. The thing to watch is that familiarity can feel like chemistry to you. Someone laughs like your dad, or has the same quiet way your first love had, and you're halfway in before you've found out who they actually are. I see this a lot with a mid-Scorpio Sun. It isn't always a problem, but it's worth asking early whether you're responding to them or to someone they remind you of. Once you're committed, anniversaries matter more than you let on. A forgotten one hurts, and you'll say it's fine.

You do well anywhere that values memory and doesn't rush people. A lot of people with the Sun here end up somewhere with long tenure, the family business, the school they went to, the hospital ward where they know every regular by name. The Sun wants to be recognised, and at work that usually happens because you're the one who knows why things are done the way they are. You were there when it was decided. Restoration of any kind suits you, furniture, old houses, archives. So does work with young children or the very old, where remembering small things about people counts for a lot. The snag is loyalty past its use-by date. You'll stay in a job for years because of a manager who left in 2019, telling yourself it's still the same place. Every couple of years, ask honestly whether you'd apply for it again.

At twenty this slice is often nostalgic already, which surprises people. You're missing being sixteen while you're still in your first share house, keeping every note and holding a couple of grudges very tightly. By the mid-thirties most people with the Sun here have learned the difference between keeping something and clinging to it, usually the hard way, after a friendship or a relationship that was only really alive in memory. The box of keepsakes gets smaller, and what's left in it gets looked at more often. The fifties tend to bring a softer version. You become the one who holds the family photos, patches up old rifts and takes younger people under your wing, and you mind less when someone changes on you, because you've changed a fair bit yourself.

Once a month, send one message to someone from an older part of your life. Name one specific thing you remember about them, the song they always put on, the way they laughed before they got to the punchline, and don't push to catch up. Then ask one question about their life as it is now, where they're living, what's keeping them busy. When they answer, reply to what they said about now, and leave the old days out of it.
